Shared SG clock-crossing FIFO (axis_cdcsync_v1) re-delivers its current word to every ready generator while any other generator is not ready: fifo_rd_en = AND of all readies, per-output valid = !empty, no per-output "already taken" bit. A backed-up SG makes the OTHER SGs replay the same command over and over.
scope: shared RTL (not an emulator model). Present in r23 firmware (axis_cdcsync_v1_0, N=4, feeds SGv6 0-3); r25 spinQICK has no SG cdcsync (SGs on tProc clock), only a readout one (N=3)
evidence: T11: SG1 got 2 commands at E2 but accepted 656 at E3 (0x0560 x654) and started 640 at E4, while SG0 was backed up (40 overlapping pulses)
impact: Corrects C8: a backed-up SG does not just stall the others, it corrupts them. Reference invalid whenever ANY SG sharing the CDC backs up; adapter/testbench must keep every SG below its FIFO depth.

finding: SGv6 has no hardware guard on pulse length: its FSM leaves a pulse when the 16-bit countdown equals 2, so nsamp=0 or 1 wraps and plays ~65536 cycles (109.4 us) instead of 0/1. nsamp>=2 is exact. QICK guards this only in software (asm_v2.py:1729-1732: min 3 cycles, max 2**16).
scope: shared RTL (kept hardware). The guard lives in the QICK compiler, which a RISC-Q toolchain/adapter would bypass
evidence: runs/nsamp_edge/len{0,1,2,3}: T1 with the LEN field patched; output on 65536 / 65537 / 2 / 3 sg_clk
impact: Adapter/RISC-Q path must enforce 3 <= nsamp < 2**16 itself. A 109 us stuck pulse also blocks that SG queue (and, via the shared CDC, can trigger F8). F1 can emit an all-zero command, which on hardware would become such a pulse.
